title: How Often Should I Get a Haircut? A Barber’s Advice for Finding Your Schedule
description: How often should you get a haircut? Saskatoon barber Cristian Perdomo shares advice for fades, medium-length hair, and schedules that fit your lifestyle.
html:
How often you should get a haircut depends on your hairstyle, your work, and your lifestyle. As a barber, I usually recommend every one to three weeks for a skin fade and every three to six weeks for a medium-length haircut.

But those ranges are a starting point. When a client sits in my chair at House of Havana in Saskatoon, I want to understand how they live, how they wear their hair, and how much maintenance they want to commit to.

Someone who wants a sharp fade every day needs a different schedule from someone who likes a longer, relaxed style. The goal is to find a routine that keeps your haircut looking good and works with your life.

How Often Should You Get a Fade?

For a fade that goes down to the skin, I recommend getting a haircut every one to two weeks if you want to maintain that fresh contrast. Three weeks is usually the longest I recommend between appointments for clients who want to keep the fade looking sharp.

A skin fade gets much of its definition from the contrast between the shortest hair on the sides and the longer hair above it. As the sides grow, that contrast softens. Your haircut may still look good, but it will look different from the day you left the barbershop.

If you are deciding between the two styles, read our guide to fade vs taper haircuts to understand how their shape and maintenance needs differ.

Every Week for a Consistently Fresh Fade

If you love the look of freshly cut sides and a clean outline, a weekly appointment may suit you.

Some clients put a high priority on that freshly groomed appearance. It is part of how they like to present themselves, whether they are at work, meeting people, or going about their day.

Every Two Weeks for Regular Maintenance

Every two weeks is a schedule I often recommend for clients who want to keep their fade looking fresh without coming in every week.

It gives us a regular opportunity to maintain the shape, clean up the edges, and keep the haircut easy to manage.

Every Three Weeks When Your Lifestyle Calls for It

For some clients, three weeks is the right fit. Their work schedule, availability, or preferences make that interval more practical.

I explain that the fade will soften as it grows. If they are comfortable with that and the overall haircut still works for them, we can build their appointments around it.

How Often Should You Cut Medium-Length Hair?

For medium-length styles, I generally recommend a haircut every three to six weeks.

This includes styles such as:

  • Modern mullets
  • Brush backs and flow hairstyles
  • Middle parts
  • Hockey flow haircuts
  • Longer styles with a more square shape

These haircuts have more length to work with and can grow out nicely when the shape is right. They do not depend on the same freshly shaved contrast as a skin fade.

That does not mean you should wait until the haircut becomes difficult to manage. We still need to maintain its balance and shape.

Choose the Shorter End if Your Hair Loses Its Shape Quickly

If your hair starts feeling puffy, becomes harder to style, or stops sitting the way you like, an appointment closer to every three weeks may make sense.

The calendar gives you a guideline, but how the haircut behaves at home matters just as much.

Allow More Time if the Haircut Still Sits Well

If you enjoy the extra length and can still style your hair easily, you may be comfortable going closer to six weeks.

I want clients to understand the difference between enjoying a haircut as it grows and struggling with one that has lost its shape.

Why Your Work and Lifestyle Matter

Your haircut schedule has to work outside the barbershop.

What you do for a living, how often you are away from home, and how you want to present yourself all influence my recommendation. A schedule that sounds ideal is not helpful if you cannot realistically keep it.

A Real Client Example: A Mining Work Schedule

One of my clients wears a mid fade with the top combed to the side. He works in the mining industry up north, spending two weeks at work followed by two weeks off.

For him, we settled on a haircut every three weeks. It is the interval we have found works well with his haircut, hair type, and lifestyle.

His work rotation is an important part of that conversation. We plan his appointments with his availability in mind so he has time for his haircut and can maintain the appearance he wants.

This is why I do not give every client the same answer. I want to find a schedule they can actually follow.

Signs It Is Time for a Haircut

Sometimes you can tell you need a haircut before you look at the date of your next appointment.

I tell clients to pay attention to how they feel when they look in the mirror and what happens when they style their hair in the morning.

Common signs include:

  • Your hair is becoming harder to style.
  • It looks too puffy or bulky.
  • Hair is growing over your ears.
  • Your hairline and outline no longer look defined.
  • The hair around your neck is growing out unevenly.
  • Your usual style no longer sits the way you want.

I sometimes joke that when the hair around your neck starts making you look like a wolf, it is probably time to come in.

But difficulty styling your hair is one of the most useful signs. If a haircut that used to be easy suddenly takes much more effort, bring that up with your barber. That information helps us decide whether your appointment schedule needs adjusting.

Why I Believe Regular Haircuts Have Value

One thing I wish more clients understood is the value of maintaining their appearance.

In my experience working with men in Saskatoon, the conversation can focus heavily on the cost of a haircut and less on what it contributes to how someone feels and presents themselves.

My opinion is that grooming deserves a place in your routine. Your haircut is part of how you show up in the world. You only get one chance to make a first impression, and looking well groomed can help you feel prepared for it.

That does not mean everyone needs a weekly appointment. It means finding a level of maintenance that matches how you want to look and making room for it.

What if Time or Budget Makes Regular Haircuts Difficult?

Be honest with your barber about what you can maintain. Your time and budget should be part of the conversation from the beginning.

Ask About Memberships or Maintenance Options

If you want to come in more frequently but cost is a concern, ask whether your barbershop offers a membership or another option for regular clients.

Every shop operates differently, so do not assume a discount is available. Have the conversation and find out what options exist.

You can also use that discussion to make sure the haircut and maintenance schedule you choose are realistic for you.

Book Your Appointments Ahead of Time

If time is the main challenge, my advice is to book ahead.

When an appointment is already in your calendar, you can plan around it and give it priority. Waiting until your hair becomes frustrating often means trying to fit a haircut into an already busy week.

Before you leave the barbershop, discuss when you should return and book a time that works with your schedule. You can also explore our haircut and grooming services in Saskatoon to choose the right service for your next visit.

How to Find Your Ideal Haircut Schedule

Start with the haircut you wear, then adjust based on how it grows and what your life allows.

My usual recommendations are:

  • Skin fades: every one to two weeks for a fresh look, with three weeks generally the longest interval I recommend for maintaining that sharp appearance.
  • Medium-length styles: every three to six weeks, depending on the shape and how easily you can style your hair.
  • Busy or rotating work schedules: plan appointments around your availability and discuss the tradeoffs with your barber.

Pay attention between visits. When does your hair start feeling too bulky? When does styling become difficult? At what point do you stop liking how it looks?

Tell your barber those details at your next appointment. They help us give you advice based on your actual experience.

At House of Havana in Saskatoon, that conversation is part of finding the right haircut for you. The aim is a style you enjoy wearing and a schedule that helps you maintain it.
